evidence.quote: metric totals in Query Shape Insights may appear significantly different than before the upgrade. This difference reflects the change in sampling method, not a change in your cluster's workload.
Query shape metrics (prefixed `mongodb.atlas.querystats`) carry `samplingstrategy` and `samplingrate` tags that describe how MongoDB Atlas collected the underlying operations:
`samplingstrategy:rate_limited`: On earlier versions, Atlas records up to a maximum number of read queries per second per host (100 per second by default), and write operations are not collected.
query shape metrics reflect a random sample of read and write operations, so metric values represent only the sampled operations.

edits.old: The MongoDB query-stats implementation groups executions in an in-memory store, with dimensions beyond query shape. Specifying batchSize can create a separate entry even when the query shape is the same; bounded LRU partitions can evict old entries. Raw store entries should not be assumed to correspond one-to-one to Atlas shape rows. (low confidence)
edits.new: The MongoDB query-stats implementation groups executions in a partitioned hash table (the QueryStatsStore) whose key has dimensions beyond query shape; the $queryStats statistics are held in an in-memory virtual collection. Specifying batchSize creates a separate store entry even when the query shape is the same, and each partition is an LRU cache that evicts the least recently used entries when over its size limit. Sources: https://github.com/mongodb/mongo/blob/master/src/mongo/db/query/query_stats/README.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/queryStats.md

evidence.quote:
The query stats store has more dimensions (i.e. more granularity) to group incoming queries than
just the query shape.

There are two distinct query stats store entries here - both the examples which include the batch
size will be treated separately from the example which does not specify a batch size.

Each partition is an LRU cache,
therefore, if adding a new entry to the partition makes it go over its size limit, the least
recently used entries will be evicted to drop below the max size.
Statistics for the `$queryStats` stage are tracked in a virtual collection that is stored in-memory.

edits.old: Percona independently advises checking custom $queryStats consumers before a MongoDB 9.0 upgrade because output structure and serialization changed. Its analysis emphasizes that read-only visibility can miss write-heavy resource use; this scopes the older Atlas 8.x read-only shape view. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-09)
edits.new: Percona advises checking tooling that consumes $queryStats before upgrading to MongoDB 9.0, because the structure and serialization of the output changed. Percona also notes that in 9.0 $queryStats covers inserts, updates and deletes, and that looking only at reads can miss write-heavy workloads. Separately, Atlas documents that on MongoDB 8.x clusters Query Shape Insights records only reads and does not collect write operations, while on 9.0 or later it samples reads and writes. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/mongodb-9-0-more-8-4-than-9-0/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/query-shape-insights.md

evidence.quote: If you already have tooling consuming $queryStats, however, check it before upgrading. The structure and serialization of the output have changed in 9.0.
In 9.0, query statistics cover inserts, updates, and deletes in addition to reads.
On clusters running MongoDB 8.x, Atlas records up to 100 read queries per second on each host. Atlas does not collect write operations.
This method also collects write operations (`insert`, `update`, and `delete`), which appear in Query Shape Insights alongside read operations.
